item.title: Cross-Layer Characterization and AI-Assisted Diagnosis of C-to-Rust Performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.33490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Migrating C code to Rust can significantly improve software security, but understanding the performance implications of such migrations remains challenging. While Rust is often claimed to match C's performance, runtime safety checks, compiler optimizations, and hardware microarchitecture interact in ways that complicate performance diagnosis. We first conduct a systematic cross-layer characterization of 12 benchmarks comprising C implementations and their Rust counterparts. Our study reveals that runtime safety checks do not necessarily dominate performance overhead, as compiler and microarchitectural optimizations often mitigate their costs. Across 8 of the 12 benchmarks, at least one Rust implementation performs within 10% of its C counterpart or outperforms it. Motivated by these findings, we introduce FerroScope, an AI-assisted performance debugger that integrates source-level analysis, compiler optimization remarks, dynamic instruction traces, and hardware performance counters to diagnose performance differences between C and Rust. FerroScope reproduces our manual findings while providing more precise explanations in several cases, including identifying compiler optimizations inhibited by redundant bounds checks. Guided by these diagnoses, we develop an LLVM compiler pass that hoists redundant bounds checks through guarded loop versioning while preserving Rust's panic behavior. The pass enables downstream compiler optimizations, including loop unrolling and conditional-move conversion, reducing Selection Sort's overhead from 2.95x to 1.00x and improving Merge Sort from 1.43x to 0.91x relative to C. Together, our results demonstrate how cross-layer performance characterization and AI-assisted diagnosis can guide safety-preserving compiler optimizations for efficient C-to-Rust migration.
item.dc:creator: Dalton Davis, Kunal Pai, Tapti Palit

item.title: Same Seed, Different Top Prediction: Cross-Platform Reproducibility of AlphaFold 3 Inference on TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs
item.description: arXiv:2611.34462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AlphaFold 3 returns the highest-ranked of several sampled structures and computes each prediction on one device. Computing centers may schedule them on different GPU types or CPU nodes. Floating-point results can differ between devices, so the same input and seed may return another structure. Neither AlphaFold 3's documentation nor its outputs warn of this. We measure how often the device changes the returned structure, and tell users what to report and how to make devices agree. We used identical inputs, weights, seeds, and settings on two Google tensor processing unit (TPU) generations (v5e, v6e), three NVIDIA GPUs (L4, A100, H100), and an Intel Xeon CPU. On 60 protein-ligand complexes, with five seeds each, switching TPU generations changed the top-ranked sample in 18.0% of 300 predictions. Recompiling never changed it on either TPU, but did so in 7.3% on the L4 GPU. Yet the structures barely moved. The top-ranked pose switched between correct and incorrect in 3.3% to 3.7% of predictions, against about 10% for a new seed. These switches nearly always came from one validity check, with the ligand within 2 angstroms. Follow-ups found the effect again on 72 new targets and between the TPUs and the CPU. Between the A100 and H100 it exceeded recompilation, although AlphaFold 3's developers verified its numerical accuracy on both. An exploratory analysis links the changes to near-tied candidates. We recommend reporting the device and every near-tied sample. A float32 trunk with full-precision matrix products made all five accelerators agree on nearly every prediction.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Pazienza

item.title: PipeAxes: Decoupling Compute and Communication Granularities for Pipeline-Parallel LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.34615v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pipeline parallelism can serve long-context language models on PCIe servers and across heterogeneous GPU clusters. Existing engines split prefill into token chunks to limit decode stalls. The chunk size also sets the GPU batch width and the size of activation transfers between stages. Small chunks reload model weights more often. Large chunks can keep the GPU and the link busy long enough to delay interactive requests. PipeAxes runs wide prefill batches a few layers at a time so decodes can run between slices. A fused Triton Hadamard-INT4 codec compresses activations, which travel in independently sized row groups over parallel TCP sockets. The scheduler uses latency slack to choose batch width, slice depth, and row-group size. We evaluated PipeAxes in 97 replays covering 5,016 requests on A800, RTX 4090, and RTX 3090 GPUs. All 74 requests met their latency targets during a tenfold bandwidth swing. In a four-stage mixture-of-experts pipeline, PipeAxes served requests within their latency targets at 23.3x the rate of calibrated Revisit-PP and 4.44x the rate of Fixed-4096 with Express. In a mixed 64K-context workload, p95 time to first token for short requests fell from 129.8 s with native vLLM to 512 ms. With INT4 transport, MMLU accuracy rose by 0.06 percentage points and GSM8K accuracy fell by 0.46 percentage points relative to BF16.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoqiang Guo, Yifan Lin, Yang Liu, Jianan Zhang, Yingqi Peng, Jiamei Lv, Yi Gao, Wei Dong

item.title: A Survey of Miss-Ratio Curve Construction Techniques
item.description: arXiv:1804.01972v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Miss ratio curve (MRC), or equivalently hit ratio curve (HRC), construction techniques have gathered the attention of many researchers. Advances in sampling now allow these curves to be approximated in constant space, which makes online working-set-size (WSS) measurement practical. Techniques span the algorithmic design paradigm from classic stack processing to compiler analysis and machine learning. Our survey produces a broad classification of the techniques based primarily on \emph{what} locality metric is recorded and \emph{how} that metric is stored for processing. Applications of these curves span from dynamic cache partitioning in the processor, to slab allocation in key-value caches, to memory tiering at the operating system level. Our survey gives an overview of the historical, exact MRC construction methods, and compares them with the state-of-the-art methods present in today's literature. This revised version improves our coverage of existing techniques and adds the techniques published since 2017 (including methods for non-LRU and multi-tier caches), the unification of the reuse time models, and a short introduction to writeback ratio curves. Finally, we revisit the open problems posed in the first version and show where there are still open areas of research.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Byrne

item.title: Toward Energy-Efficient and Low-Power Arrhythmia Detection for Wearable Devices
item.description: arXiv:2607.14747v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, and conditions such as arrhythmia often require long-term monitoring for effective detection and diagnosis. However, current wearable monitoring devices are bulky, uncomfortable, and typically rely on clinicians to manually evaluate electrocardiograms (ECGs). While Deep Learning (DL) algorithms have shown superior performance in arrhythmia detection and classification, their computational complexity coupled with high power consumption limit deployment in wearable devices. To address this challenge, this paper investigates the use of approximation techniques to reduce the power and energy consumption of DL architectures while maintaining acceptable classification performance. Specifically, techniques such as data precision reduction and approximate multiplication are investigated in a state-of-the-art DL model and its corresponding hardware architecture. The model is trained and validated using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, and hardware implementations employing various approximate multipliers are synthesized and evaluated. Compared with the state-of-the-art 8.75 {\mu}W (and 2.08 {\mu}J) reference architecture, our proposed architecture consumes 3.07 {\mu}W (and 2.17 {\mu}J) at 12 kHz, showing 64.9% reduction in power consumption while providing an acceptable output quality, i.e., 93.7% classification accuracy and 92.1% sensitivity. At 100 MHz, our proposed architecture consumes 9.45 mW (and 0.8 {\mu}J), showing 61.5% reduction in energy consumption as compared to the state-of-the-art architecture. These results demonstrate that our proposed approximations significantly extend wearable device battery life while preserving the required arrhythmia classification performance.
item.dc:creator: Floriaan Bulten, Yawar Rasheed, Arlene John, Vincenzo Stoico, Ghayoor Gillani
